title: Determination of dimethylsulfoniopropionate and dimethylsulfoxide in Posidonia oceanica leaf tissue
author: Champenois, Borges
materials: Statistical analysis was made with Graphpad Prism3.

steps.title: Collect leaf sections
steps.instruction: Dive to collect Posidonia oceanica leaves in triplicate, cut a 10 cm section from the bottom of each leaf, remove epiphytes with a razor blade, and freeze immediately at –20 °C.

steps.title: Prepare leaf tissue
steps.instruction: Remove frozen samples, blot away melt water with absorbent paper, cut the leaf pieces with stainless‑steel scissors into 3 × 3 mm squares, and thoroughly mix the fragments.

steps.title: Weigh sample into vial
steps.instruction: Weigh approximately 20 mg of the mixed tissue into a pre‑weighed 20 mL borosilicate vial.

steps.title: Add water and NaOH
steps.instruction: Add 2.5 mL of Milli‑Q water followed by 2.5 mL of 12 M NaOH (same solution used for standards) to the vial; this introduces ~0.05 % ionic strength, which is considered negligible for headspace equilibrium.

steps.title: Seal vial
steps.instruction: Immediately seal the vial; from this point standards and samples are processed identically.

steps.title: Test for free DMS (optional)
steps.instruction: Place ~100 mg leaf tissue in a 20 mL vial with 5 mL Milli‑Q water, seal, sonicate for 2 h to rupture cell walls, withdraw 100 µL of headspace (10× the normal volume) and inject into the GC to verify that DMS is below detection.

steps.title: Headspace sampling and GC injection
steps.instruction: Using a gas‑tight 10 µL Hamilton syringe, withdraw 10 µL of headspace gas from each sealed vial and inject it into the gas chromatograph for quantification of DMSP and DMSO.

description: Posidonia oceanica is an endemic keystone specie of the Mediterranean coast. This macrophyte is able to produce dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) [1,2]. The role of DMSP in the P. oceanica remains unclear. Otte et al [3] listed different roles for DMSP in macrophytes: methylation, detoxification of sediment by removal of sulphide and reduction of overflow of energy, cryoprotectant or osmoregulation. In the case of P. oceanica, DMSP cannot act as osmolyte because this macrophyte is stenohalin. Similarly, DMSP cannot act as a cryoprotectant because P. oceanica is endemic of the Mediterranean Sea where water never freezes. DMSP is the precursor of dimethyl sulfide (DMS) and acrylic acid; these two compounds can act as herbivore deterrent for macrophytes [3]. DMSP acts as antioxidant in marine phytoplankton [4] and higher plants such as Spartina alterniflora [5], and in both cases DMSP is oxidized to dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO). Mcfarlin and Alber [6] suggested that the DMSO:DMSP ratio can be used as an indicator of stress of S. alterniflora for a variety of disturbances. The aim of this paper is to describe a method to accurately measure the DMSP:DMSO ratio in P. oceanica tissues with the possible goal of using this ratio as a stress indicator for this macrophyte by analogy with S. alterniflora. The method we propose here is an adaptation of DMS(P,O) analytical method that is used typically for phytoplankton [7], that was adapted for P. oceanica leaf tissue, and is based on the headspace technique, instead of purge-and-trap. Fig. 1 show the calibration curves for DMSP and DMSO based on the mixtures of DMSP and DMSO given in Table 1. We can see on Fig. 1a that the response of the FPD to the DMS concentration is sigmoidal. If we restrict the calibration to DMS concentration from 0 to 80 μmol L−1 (n = 7), we can use a polynomial second order model to fit the calibration curve, with a determination coefficient (R2) of 0.989.
